title: Combination Sum
prompt:
Given an array of distinct positive numbers candidates and a target, return every unique combination of candidates that adds up to target. You may use the same candidate as many times as you like. Two combinations are the same if they use the same numbers the same number of times, so [2,2,3] and [3,2,2] count once.

Write combinationSum(candidates, target). Order does not matter, inside or between combinations.

combinationSum([2, 3, 6, 7], 7);   // [[2,2,3], [7]]
combinationSum([2, 3, 5], 8);      // [[2,2,2,2], [2,3,3], [3,5]]
combinationSum([2], 1);            // []

Constraints: up to 30 candidates, each between 2 and 40; target between 1 and 40.

tests.name: [2,3,6,7] target 7
tests.code:
function norm(lists) { return lists.map((l) => [...l].sort((a, b) => a - b)).map((l) => JSON.stringify(l)).sort(); }
assertEqual(norm(combinationSum([2,3,6,7], 7)), norm([[2,2,3],[7]]));

tests.name: [2,3,5] target 8
tests.code:
function norm(lists) { return lists.map((l) => [...l].sort((a, b) => a - b)).map((l) => JSON.stringify(l)).sort(); }
assertEqual(norm(combinationSum([2,3,5], 8)), norm([[2,2,2,2],[2,3,3],[3,5]]));

tests.name: a candidate equal to the target
unsorted input, no duplicate combinations
counts the 4 ways to make 10 from [2,3,5]

hints: Trigger: "all combinations that sum to target". You must list them, not just count them, so it is backtracking (if it only asked how many, DP would be faster).

Idea: carry remaining = target - sum(current). At 0, record. Loop over candidates from start; recursing with the same index i allows reuse, and never looking left of start stops [2,3] and [3,2] both appearing. Sort first so you can break as soon as a candidate is bigger than remaining.

Code shape: function explore(start, remaining) { if (remaining === 0) { result.push([...current]); return; } for (let i = start; i < sorted.length; i++) { if (sorted[i] > remaining) break; current.push(sorted[i]); explore(i, remaining - sorted[i]); current.pop(); } }
explain:
Time: exponential in the worst case, roughly O(ntarget / smallest candidate), but pruning (sorted + break) cuts most branches. Space O(target / smallest candidate) for the recursion depth, plus the output.

Say it: "I need to list every combination, so I'll backtrack with a start index and the remaining amount. Recursing on the same index allows reuse; never going left avoids duplicate orderings; sorting lets me stop the loop as soon as a candidate overshoots." Follow-up you may get: "What if I only want the number of combinations?" Answer: that is the coin change ways DP, O(n × target).
